newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FOCUS - Russia row sours record De Beers year.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Russia row sours record De Beers year.

text.p: South African diamond giant De Beers said on Wednesday that sales of uncut stones hit a record high in 1996, but the news was overshadowed by a showdown with Russia which knocked two percent off the share price.
De Beers gave an ultimatum to Russia, threatening to stop doing business next year under the terms of an interim deal unless Moscow signed a new agreement.
"De Beers...is not prepared to continue to buy diamonds under the old agreement beyond 31 December 1996," the company said in a statement.

The two sides have been in protracted talks on a new agreement to market Russian diamonds through De Beers' Central Selling Organisation (CSO) marketing cartel, which controls some 75 percent of all trade in rough diamonds.
Russia accounts for about 20 percent of total CSO sales.
Russia's Itar-Tass news agency quoted an unidentified Finance Ministry official as saying on Wednesday that Moscow was ready to continue working with De Beers.
But it also quoted the official as having said that a De Beers announcement giving Russia until the end of the year to sign a formal trade agreement was "indadequate".
The official said the ministry had not received De Beers' announcement.
CSO managing director Gary Ralfe said the interim arrangements had not worked, with a a large quantity of Russia gems leaking onto the international market.
"In addition to goods out of the stockpile we have also seen current production leaking out," he told a news conference.

As a result, De Beers said it would be reviewing its relationship with the Russian authorities in 1997, although it still hoped the Russian government would ratify the new trade agreement "in due course".
In the meantime, Ralfe said De Beers would be buying Russian diamonds from a variety of sources next year.
"We will be free...to buy Russian diamonds on the basis that we and them can agree -- a willing buyer, willing seller."

Prospects for a new deal had looked bright back in February when a memorandum of understanding was signed. But final approval has been bogged down by clashes within Russia between different factions in the diamond industry.
Stock analysts said it was unlikely Moscow would sign up by the end of the month, but some remained hopeful the De Beers' sabre-rattling would work.
"This (the ultimatum) will heighten the urgency of sorting out the problems," said Des Mayers, analyst at stockbrokers G O'Flaherty.
The row unnerved investors, triggering a three rand loss in the De Beers share price on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange to 129.50 rand.
"The shares are being sold on the back of the Russian news...but the share should remain underpinned by the record sales," one dealer said.

De Beers said rough diamond sales by the CSO rose seven percent to $4.834 billion in 1996 from $4.531 billion in 1995, reflecting continuing strength in world retail demand for diamond jewellery, particularly in the United States.
Retail sales of diamond jewellery in 1995 rose on average by an estimated five percent to a record level, with the U.S. market increasing by eight percent.

The CSO, which has its headquarters in London, sells rough diamonds to a select group of dealers at so-called "sights" which take place 10 times per year. The final sight of 1996 took place last week.
